turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come in, take a seat. What's the problem?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): My big toe, doc. It's been absolutely killing me since last night. I hardly slept a wink.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Which side?

[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. It's swollen right up, red, hot, and I can't get a sock on it. Is this gout? My uncle had gout and they reckoned it was the worst pain going, and I'm scared it's an infection because it came on so fast and—
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): One thing at a time. Fever?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Would a fever mean it's in the blood? I was reading—
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes or no.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I don't think so. I feel a bit washed out, that's all.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Nausea or vomiting?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): When did the pain start?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, can I just ask, if I leave it will it spread up the foot? I've got work—
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): When.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Last night. I was right at tea, then about ten, watching the footy, it started throbbing. Woke me whenever I drifted off.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any injury? Stub it, drop something on it?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that. I didn't knock it.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Other joints sore?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No, just this toe. Will I be able to work tomorrow? I'm on my feet all day at the warehouse and—
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll sort that. Knees or back playing up?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Happened before?

[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, same toe about a year back, and it settled in a few days. I just took Panadol and rested, probably should've come in. This time's worse, I was nearly crying this morning.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Pain out of ten?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): A nine. Maybe a ten if I bump it. What number means I should be in hospital? Because if it's a ten—
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Nine is enough, you're in the right place. Medicines?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): A water tablet, for my blood pressure. Couple of years now.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Which one, what dose?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Hydrochlorothiazide. Um, twelve and a half milligrams, mornings.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): File here says twenty-five milligrams.
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Nah, it's the half tablet, twelve point five. They dropped it. Unless the chemist switched me back and I didn't clock it. Now you've got me doubting myself.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll call the dose unclear. Anything else — aspirin, Nurofen?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): No, just that, and Panadol sometimes. Is the water tablet causing this, and should I stop it? I don't want my pressure going through the roof.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Don't stop it. Allergies to medicines?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Not that I know of. What if I'm allergic to whatever you give me and I don't know yet? That can happen, right?
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll stick to something straightforward. Do you drink?

[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Beer on weekends, Saturday mainly, four or five stubbies, sometimes a couple more at a barbie on the Sunday, not through the week. I had a few Saturday. Is that what did this, because it was days ago, how can it hit overnight?
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alcohol can bump the uric acid up, yes. Smoke?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Never have. And I walk a fair bit at work, if that matters. Does exercise make gout worse? Should I be resting completely?
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Rest this foot. Right big toe is hot, red and swollen over the MTP joint, very tender to touch, and the skin's not broken. Foot pulses are present.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): So it's gout, isn't it? Just say it. And how long till the swelling goes? I've got a shift tomorrow I really can't miss, they're short-staffed and—
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Most likely an acute gout flare. I can't be certain till we see the bloods. Infection is less likely — no fever, skin intact.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Bloods, what bloods, and do I have to fast? I hate needles. How big is it, and when do you get the result?
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Serum uric acid, and kidney function because of the fluid tablet. No fasting. Result in a day or two.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Alright. Can I just use the Nurofen I've got at home?
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): I was going to give you naproxen, five hundred milligrams twice a day, for five days.

[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Naproxen — that's an anti-inflammatory, yeah? Because I get shocking heartburn, and when I had the scope they told me to stay off those. I should've said. The scope was for the reflux, two years back... or three, I can never remember which.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): That changes it. No naproxen. Colchicine instead.

[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Colchicine. That's the one that gives you diarrhoea, isn't it? My mate couldn't leave the toilet. How many do I take, is it safe with the water tablet, and can I have a beer this weekend or is that completely out?

[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Five hundred micrograms, one tablet, twice a day, for three days, then stop. Diarrhoea, stop and ring the clinic. It's fine with the fluid tablet. No beer till this settles, and cut back the weekend drinking after.

[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Only three days? What if it's still agony on day four? And my pressure — last time at the chemist they said one-fifty over ninety-something. If I keep the tablet will that number climb because of the pain?

[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Keep taking the water tablet as you have been. Pain won't meaningfully shift that reading. If the toe isn't settling in three days, come back and we'll reassess. Not adding another drug today.

[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh — the chair. Yesterday arvo I kicked the kitchen chair hard, on that same toe, and I told you I hadn't knocked it but I did. It stung for a minute and I forgot all about it. So is this just a bruise, not gout?
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): It may have stirred the joint up. Doesn't change the treatment. We still treat it as gout.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): You're not worried it's broken? Don't I need an x-ray now you've heard that? What if I walk on a fracture all week?
[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): No x-ray today. If it's not improving we can image it then.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. The blood test — do I go now? Will you ring me? If the uric acid comes back normal, does that mean it isn't gout after all?
[SEG0057] person_1 (DOCTOR): A normal uric acid during a flare doesn't fully rule gout out. Pathology's down the hall, form's with this. I'll see you in a week regardless, sooner if it worsens.
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): A week. What about tonight, for the pain? Is Panadol alright with the colchicine? How many?
[SEG0059] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes. Two five-hundred-milligram tablets, up to four times a day. Foot up, ice wrapped in a tea towel, not straight on the skin.
[SEG0060] person_2 (PATIENT): And work tomorrow? If I rest it today can I do a shorter shift, or will I make it worse? I can't afford to—
[SEG0061] person_1 (DOCTOR): Don't do the warehouse shift tomorrow. Rest. A day off the feet matters more than pushing through.

[SEG0062] person_2 (PATIENT): Right. So colchicine three days, Panadol, ice, elevate, no beer, keep the fluid tablet, bloods today, back in a week, no x-ray unless it's not settling. Did I get that right? Sorry, I'm all over the place.
[SEG0063] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's right. Script goes to your chemist electronically. Start the colchicine today.
[SEG0064] person_2 (PATIENT): What if I get chest pain or the red spreads? You didn't say what the danger signs are and that's the bit that worries me most.
[SEG0065] person_1 (DOCTOR): Diarrhoea that won't stop, redness climbing the foot, or you feel properly unwell — come back or go to emergency. Chest pain, same thing, don't sit on it.
[SEG0066] person_2 (PATIENT): Chest pain from a toe tablet? Is colchicine bad for the heart? I need you to say it plainly.
[SEG0067] person_1 (DOCTOR): No. That's a general safety-net, not a colchicine effect. You're right to start it. Off you go.

spec.situation: Man with a very painful swollen big toe since last night; drinks beer at weekends, takes a water tablet; had the same 'a year back'; says no injury then recalls kicking a chair; colchicine or NSAID plan; blood uric acid test.
features: doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.
disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.
interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.

denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.

bad.reason: Reflux mentioned historically; ongoing status not stated.
Kick to same toe yesterday afternoon supported; status should be past event, not present symptom.

omissions.text: Hydrochlorothiazide dose was stated as 12.5 mg each morning by the patient, with the chart listing 25 mg; the current recorded medication entry omits the dose entirely.

The patient denied any injury initially, then later corrected this and reported kicking a kitchen chair hard on the same toe yesterday afternoon; this contradiction should be captured as an uncertainty/disagreement rather than simply recording the injury as present.
The prior same-toe episode about a year ago was treated with Panadol and rest and the patient said he probably should have come in; this is additional detail to the past episode history.
Naproxen 500 mg twice a day for 5 days was initially planned, then cancelled after the patient disclosed severe heartburn/reflux and being told after an endoscopy to avoid anti-inflammatories/NSAIDs.
The patient reported being told after a previous scope/endoscopy to stay off anti-inflammatories because of reflux/heartburn; this medication intolerance/avoidance advice is not recorded.
The doctor advised no fasting for the blood tests and said results would be available in a day or two.
